7. Complete medication list and details on Crohn’s disease activity and current treatments (steroids, biologics).
8. History for systemic symptoms (fever, chills), social history (smoking, IV drug use), and any prior skin cancers.

Obtain these data before confirming pyoderma gangrenosum. If biopsy shows compatible neutrophilic dermatosis and cultures/imaging exclude infection/osteomyelitis/vascular disease and malignancy, then PG would be a defensible diagnosis.

[THOUGHT] Analysis:
The history and course (painful ulcer that began as a pustule, marked worsening after bedside debridement consistent with pathergy, association with Crohn’s disease) plus the described lesion morphology (violaceous rolled borders, cribriform base) are highly suggestive of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Crucially, the case includes extensive negative workup that addresses the major alternative diagnoses: normal deep tissue cultures (bacterial/mycobacterial/fungal), negative special stains, “deep” biopsy of the ulcer edge/base without evidence of malignancy or vasculitis, normal inflammatory markers and HbA1c, normal vascular studies (ABI/duplex), and normal MRI ruling out osteomyelitis. Those exclusions materially strengthen the clinical diagnosis of PG, which is a diagnosis of exclusion.

Missing or uncertain items (not fatal to the diagnosis but potentially relevant):
- Documentation of current medications/immunosuppressive or steroid therapy and precise Crohn’s disease activity (relevant for management and prognosis, not necessary to establish diagnosis).
- Photographic documentation and precise wound measurements would be helpful but are not required given the described morphology.
- Histopathology for PG can be non-specific; the reported “normal” biopsy is compatible with PG if infection/malignancy/vasculitis are excluded — biopsy adequacy (edge vs. base, depth) appears to have been acceptable per report.

Given the characteristic clinical features plus comprehensive exclusion of infectious, vascular, malignant, and osseous causes, the available information is sufficient to support the diagnosis of ulcerative pyoderma gangrenosum.
